lines.text: In 1939, Germany had a machine that could hide anything.
Orders. Ship positions. Attack plans.
You pressed a key, and a different letter lit up.
Press the same key again, and you got something else entirely.
It was called Enigma.
Every night at midnight, the settings changed.
That meant one hundred and fifty-nine quintillion possible combinations.
And whatever you'd worked out that day was now useless.
The Germans were sure it could never be broken.
They were almost right.
By 1940, German submarines were hunting in the Atlantic.
They hunted in groups. Wolf packs.
Every week, supply ships went down by the dozen.
Britain was an island. Without those ships, it would starve.
Every order to every submarine went out by radio.
Britain could hear every single message.
It just couldn't read any of them.
So Britain did something strange.
It gathered mathematicians, chess players and puzzle fanatics at a country house called Bletchley Park.
One of them was a quiet twenty-seven year old named Alan Turing.
He chained his tea mug to a radiator, so nobody could steal it.
And he had an idea that nobody liked.
Stop trying to beat the machine by hand.
Build a machine to beat it.
But there was a problem.
Even a machine couldn't check every setting before midnight.
For months, it ran. And found nothing.
Ships were still sinking. People wanted results.
Then Turing found a tiny flaw inside Enigma itself.
A letter could never turn into itself.
An A was never an A. An E was never an E.
And the German operators were predictable.
Every morning, the same weather report. The same words.
Guess one word, and almost every setting became impossible.
Quintillions of options shrank to a few thousand.
In the summer of 1940, the machine they called the Bomb stopped.
It had found the key.
From then on, Britain often read the orders before the submarines did.
Some say it shortened the war by two years.
The Germans never found out.
Their perfect machine had one tiny flaw.
And one stubborn man went looking for it.
